summary.title: Failure is inevitable: Learning from a large outage, and building for reliability in depth at Datadog
summary.one_liner: Datadog's account of its March 2023 outage and how it re-architected systems for graceful degradation: persist data early, prioritize live data, make retries and recovery tooling safer, and avoid shared-fate dependencies.
takeaways: A binary never-fail design can turn a partial outage into a full one; prefer serving partial or slightly stale but accurate results.
Persist data to disk-based storage as early as possible in the pipeline so it can be replayed after node or store failures.
Prioritize live data over backlogs, use QoS and Kubernetes PriorityClass, and make retries use backoff and dead letter queues so recovery isn't slowed.
Avoid global control systems and non-local critical dependencies, and keep break-glass tooling so recovery tools don't depend on what they are recovering.
Chaos test against degradation conditions (e.g. insufficient capacity) rather than specific failure mechanisms.
summary.summary: Datadog describes a March 2023 incident in which an unsupervised global update removed connectivity to roughly 50-60% of production Kubernetes nodes, making the platform appear fully down because its systems prioritized accuracy over partial visibility. The post argues that root-cause fixes alone are insufficient and walks through product-by-product changes: disk-based persistence at intake, prioritizing live data, safer retry and recovery logic, removing a shared Cassandra cache from the metrics path, sharding Vault, and adding break-glass tooling. It closes with patterns the team learned and reports fewer significant incidents and faster mitigation in logs since the changes.
